name: Culle
confidence_why: Adelaar (1989) states outright that he does not know where the accent falls in Culle words and that the diacritics of the only early word list (Martínez Compañón, 1780s) have no known function, Urban (2019) likewise finds those diacritics unexplained, and neither Adelaar and Muysken (2004) nor Andrade (1999) offers any stress statement, so the "undetermined" record rests on one explicit authoritative statement that nothing contradicts.

In Rodolfo Cerrón-Palomino & Gustavo Solís Fonseca (eds.), Temas de lingüística amerindia (Primer Congreso Nacional de Investigaciones Lingüístico-Filológicas), 83-105. Lima: CONCYTEC/GTZ. [Google Books volume e6hgAAAAMAAJ, excerpt view]

catalog_quote: ... mapas militares transcriben los nombres culle de lugar sin acento, excepto cuando la terminación es -gón. Ya que no sé dónde se sitúa el acento en cada caso particular, seguiré esta práctica. Dejo de lado los diacríticos empleados en la lista de Martínez Compañón porque su función es desconocida. La sugerencia de Silva Santisteban (1983: 144) de que el símbolo compuesto por č debe ser interpretado como la ch española es improbable.

Since I do not know where the accent falls in each particular case, I shall follow this practice. I leave aside the diacritics used in Martínez Compañón's list because their function is unknown.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress rule is recoverable: the principal modern analyst of Culli states that the position of the accent in Culle forms is unknown to him and that the diacritics (grave accents etc.) in the 18th-century Martínez Compañón word list, the only source that marks anything, are of unknown function. The one orthographic regularity (Spanish acute on toponyms in -gón, e.g. Chusgón) is a map-spelling convention for hispanicised place names, not a claim about Culli word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Toponyms ending in -gón are written with a (final) accent on Peruvian military maps; Adelaar adopts this spelling without endorsing it as Culli stress. Later work (Adelaar & Muysken 2004: 402 as cited by Andrade 2016; Urban 2025: 586) reads the grave-accented final <-ù> of the verbs in Martínez Compañón's list as an infinitive marker /u/~/w/, not as a stress mark; Urban 2019: 79, 104 fn.103 likewise finds the plan's diacritics unexplained and the grave-as-stress reading doubtful.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns citation of toponyms and word-list items of an extinct language known from c. 60 lexical items; no phrase- vs word-level distinction is possible. Passage reconstructed from overlapping Google Books snippets (snippet view volume), not from a full page scan.
new_statements.identity_note: Culli = Culle/Kulyi/Ilinga (Glottolog cull1235, no ISO). All sources treat the Huamachuco material (Martínez Compañón, 1780s) and the Pallasca material (Gonzales 1915 via Rivet 1949) as one language; no dialect differentiation is possible. The quoted statement is about the language as a whole (toponyms + word list), not a particular variety.

tone.quote: El ilustrativo ejemplo tomado de Reyna, sin embargo, no puede ser generalizado. En el terreno de la conjetura, postulamos que en la lengua kulli el acento agudo era canónico, pero que, al encontrarse con el quechua, este patrón comienza a desestabilizarse en razón del canónico grave del quechua, pero se vuelve a reencontrar con el canon oxítono del castellano y recupera su vigencia.
tone.locator: ch. 3, section 3.1.3 'Fenomenos suprasegmentales', closing paragraph of 3.1.3.2 'Entonacion', p. 288 (page number in footer); supporting passages: 3.1.3.1 'Acento' p. 285 ('La presencia de la acentuacion oxitona de palabras en kulli esta atestiguada en la lista de las 43 vozes de Martinez (1790) si atendemos con cuidado a los diacriticos..') and p. 203.
tone.translation: The illustrative example taken from Reyna, however, cannot be generalised. In the realm of conjecture, we postulate that in the Kulli language final (oxytone) stress was canonical, but that, on meeting Quechua, this pattern began to destabilise because of Quechua's canonical penultimate stress, and then met again with the oxytone canon of Spanish and recovered its force.
